title: Why Do Men Leave the Church, and How Do You Reach Them?
subtitle: On why men drift from the church, how to call them back, and what real discipleship of men requires beyond pancakes and platitudes

sections.title: The Half of the Pew That Is Missing
sections.body:
Look out over most congregations on a Sunday and count. The women are there. The children are there because the women brought them. The men are thinner on the ground, and the ones who came are often there because someone made them.

This is not new, and it is not an accident. The church has slowly become a place many men feel they are visiting rather than belonging.

We built services that reward sitting still and feeling things, and then we wondered why the man who frames houses and fixes engines felt like a guest in his own faith. I am not excusing the drift. A man who will not follow Christ because the music is soft is a man making excuses, and we should say so. But we are not innocent either. We made a room and then acted surprised that half the people we invited could not find themselves in it. Before we lecture men about commitment, we should ask an honest question about what we actually offered them to commit to.

sections.title: Why Men Drift
sections.body:
Men do not usually storm out of the church. They fade. They miss a Sunday for the lake, then two for the kids' sports, then they realize no one called and they conclude they were never needed.

A man stays where he is needed. A man leaves where he is merely tolerated.

Much of our ministry to men assumed they wanted to be entertained or fed. They did not. They wanted a mission worth their strength and a man worth following, and when the church offered neither, they went and found both at work, where a boss expected something of them and a paycheck told them they mattered. The deepest hunger in most men is not for a softer message. It is to be told that their life counts for something, that they were made for a fight that matters, that their failures as fathers and husbands are not the last word. We have a gospel that says exactly that. We have too often preached it as though it were addressed to no one in particular and asked nothing in return.

sections.title: Call Them to Something Costly
sections.body:
If you want to reach men, raise the bar, do not lower it. The man who will not come for coffee and a craft will come for a thing that demands his back, his courage, his word kept under pressure.

Do not invite men to a program. Summon them to a charge.

Jesus did not recruit his men with comfort. He told them to leave their boats, take up a cross, lose their lives to find them. That is the voice men were built to answer. So put a real burden in front of them. Ask the new believer to read the Gospel of Mark and report back. Ask the recovering man to mentor the one three steps behind him. Ask the strong one to carry the weak one's groceries and never mention it. Men rise to weight and shrink from fuss. Give them weight. And tell them the truth about what following Christ will cost them, because a man trusts the leader who refuses to flatter him.

sections.title: What Discipling Men Actually Looks Like
sections.body:
It is not a sermon series. It is a man and a few other men, meeting early because that is the only hour they have, reading the Bible and telling the truth about their week.

Shoulder to shoulder, not face to face. Men open up over a task, not under a spotlight.

Get them doing something together and the words will come, in the truck, on the job site, on the early run, in the half hour before the others wake. Ask the questions men never get asked. How is your marriage really. When did you last pray with your wife. What are you hiding. Are you looking at things you should not. The man who has never been asked has been waiting his whole life for someone brave enough to ask. And then keep his secrets and check his progress, because a man will let one other man into the locked room of his life only if that man proves he will not leave and will not gossip. Discipleship of men is slow, unglamorous, and almost entirely off the platform. Most of the kingdom is.

sections.title: Most Men Are Looking for a Father
sections.body:
Underneath the toughness, most men in your church are carrying a hole shaped like a father. He was absent, or harsh, or merely silent, and the boy grew into a man still aching to hear a word he never got. Well done. I am proud of you. You are going to be alright.

I grew up without a father. I know the exact weight of that absence, and I know it does not lift on its own.

You cannot be every man's father, and you should not try. But you can be the one older man who tells a younger man the truth and then stays in the room afterward. That is what most of them never had. The world is full of men who can criticize a younger man and empty of men who will believe in one. Be the rare one. Lay a hand on a shoulder and say the blessing his own father withheld. It will undo some of them, right there, because it is the thing they have wanted since they were small. We disciple men one fatherless heart at a time. There is no faster way, and there never was.
